Series::log¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::log() const -> Series
Series& Series::log_()

What It Does¶

Applies the natural logarithm elementwise.

log() is the inverse-style partner to Series::exp on positive inputs. It preserves shape and transforms each element independently.

The important point is domain sensitivity:

  • positive inputs produce finite real outputs

  • 1 maps to 0

  • values between 0 and 1 map to negative outputs

  • 0 maps to -inf

  • negative inputs map to nan

So log() is not mainly about shape or broadcasting. It is about input domain.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its natural logarithm.

Gradient¶

For positive inputs, log() has the familiar reciprocal derivative:

  • the forward value is log(x)

  • the backward multiplier is 1 / x

That means gradients become larger near zero and smaller for larger positive values.

In-Place Form¶

log_() is the in-place sibling of log(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.718281828459045});

auto& ref = x.log_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Inputs chosen to produce exact whole-number logs.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.718281828459045, 7.38905609893065}).log());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000]

Example 2. Fractions between 0 and 1 produce negative outputs.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 4.0}).log();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.3862944, -0.69314718, 0, 1.3862944]

Example 3. The reverse-mode sensitivity is the reciprocal of the positive input.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.log();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.69314718, 1.3862944]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0.5, 0.25]

Example 4. Domain edges do not throw here; they surface as special floating values.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({1.0, 0.0, -1.0}).log();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, -inf, nan]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • log() is only finite on positive inputs.

  • 0 yields -inf, which is often more dangerous in downstream arithmetic than an immediate exception because it can travel further before you notice.

  • Negative inputs yield nan.

  • Gradients become large near zero on the positive side.

Summary¶

Use log() as a domain-sensitive unary transform. The key point is not shape, but admissible values: positive inputs are ordinary, zero becomes -inf, and negatives become nan.

See Also¶

  • Series::exp: inverse-style counterpart on valid domains.

  • Series::sqrt: another domain-sensitive unary transform.

  • Series::sign: cheap sign inspection before deciding whether a log() call is sensible.
